card.stem: The eaves of a timber flat roof for a bathroom is constructed as shown in the sketch. The roof is covered with layers of bituminous felt on plywood decking on 200 mm × 50 mm roof joists. The roof is insulated and there is a plasterboard ceiling beneath. The external wall supporting the flat roof is a 350 mm concrete block wall with an insulated cavity.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the eaves of the flat roof and through the external wall. The section should show the typical construction details from 400 mm below the wallplate, through the wall, fascia, soffit and roof joists and include the roof surface. Show 1.5 metres length of roof joist and include four typical dimensions.

rows.contextNote: Any 7 of the above details ( 5 marks each). Credit the best SEVEN acceptable details at 5 marks each, capped at 35. Marked details: three layers of bituminous felt; plywood decking 25 mm; 50 × 50 mm counter battens on a firring piece; roof/ceiling joists 200 × 50 mm; at least 150 mm insulation; 12.5 mm insulated foil-backed plasterboard and skim; an airtightness seal taped to the masonry; a 100 × 75 mm wallplate with straps; a cavity barrier or non-combustible tile or slate; 15 mm internal plaster; 100 mm inner leaf; cavity insulation; 100 mm outer leaf; 19 mm render; fascia and soffit.

options: 12.5 insulated foil-backed plasterboard with skim coat
Air tightness seal taped to masonry
Proprietary cavity barrier / non combustible tile or slate
Wall insulation / cavity / full fill cavity

rows.contextNote: Four appropriate typical dimensions on the section, 1 each.

card.stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house which was built over ten years ago. The external walls of the house are 300 mm concrete block walls with an un-insulated cavity. It is proposed to improve the insulation properties of the external walls by: insulating the cavity and adding a system of insulation to the inside of the walls.
card.questionText: Using notes and neat freehand sketches, show how to apply each system of insulation to the wall. For each system of insulation, specify the insulation material used and include details of the internal surface finish of the wall.

rows.contextNote: Two valid descriptions 4 each, and the insulation type and internal finish 4. Such as: 22 mm holes drilled through the outer leaf at 800 mm horizontally and 1350 mm vertically, with extra holes under cills and over heads; polystyrene beads pumped in with a light glue by a specialist; the holes filled and painted to match.

rows.verbatim: Quality of sketch and details (excellent, good, fair)
rows.contextNote: Quality of the cavity-fill sketch and details: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

rows.verbatim: Adding a system of insulating to the inside of the walls – Notes
rows.contextNote: Two valid descriptions 4 each, and the insulation type and internal finish 4. Such as: 50 × 50 mm battens at 400 mm centres with insulation between, a vapour barrier and 12 mm plasterboard and skim; or insulated dry-lining board glued and mechanically fixed, joints taped and filled, and emulsion paint. Insulation such as fibreglass, polystyrene, polyurethane, cork, hemp or sheep’s wool.

rows.verbatim: Quality of sketch and details (excellent, good, fair)
rows.contextNote: Quality of the internal-insulation sketch and details: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

card.questionText: One corner of a trench for a strip foundation is shown in the sketch. Describe, using notes and neat freehand sketches, the setting-out of a typical strip foundation under the following headings: levelling the profiles; locating the position of the trench; squaring the corner of the trench; locating the finished level of the concrete in the foundation.

rows.contextNote: Primary communication 5 and other communication 4. Such as: profiles of two uprights and a cross rail, levelled from a secured datum point with a laser, optical or water level, the top usually at finished floor level.

rows.verbatim: Locating the position of the trench
rows.contextNote: Primary communication 5 and other communication 4. Such as: lines stretched across the profile rails at the four corners locate the outside of the wall; the wall and trench widths marked on the profiles.

rows.verbatim: Squaring the corner of the trench
rows.contextNote: Primary communication 5 and other communication 4. Such as: lines at right angles to the building line set with a 3, 4, 5 triangle; the rectangle checked by measuring the diagonals.

rows.verbatim: Locating the finished level of the concrete in the foundation
rows.contextNote: Primary communication 5 and other communication 4. Such as: pegs driven in the trench with their tops level with the top of the foundation, set by laser or with boning rods and a traveller.

card.stem: A non load-bearing stud partition separates two upstairs bedrooms in a dwelling house. The floor and partition are supported on a 215 mm solid block wall, as shown in the sketch. The floor is a floating tongued and grooved oak floor on plywood, on 200 mm × 50 mm joists with a plasterboard ceiling beneath.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the stud partition and the floor. Show the typical construction details from a level 300 mm below the plasterboard ceiling, through the wall, floor and partition to a point 400 mm above the finished floor level. Include three typical dimensions on your drawing. Note: Show a floor width of 500 mm at each side of the partition.

rows.contextNote: Any 6 of the above details ( 6 marks each). Credit the best SIX acceptable details at 6 marks each, capped at 36. Marked details: stud partition 100 × 50 mm; insulation between the studs; 12.5 mm plasterboard; 120 × 20 mm skirting; floating tongued and grooved oak floor; bubble underlay or matting; 18–25 mm plywood; 200 × 50 mm joists; at least 150 mm insulation between the joists; plasterboard, plaster and vapour barrier; 15 mm plaster; 215 mm solid block wall.

options: Floating tongued and grooved oak timber floor
Polyethylene bubble underlay or proprietary matting

rows.contextNote: Three typical dimensions, 2 each.

card.questionText: Explain with the aid of notes and neat freehand sketches, any five of the following: solar panel; dovetail halving joint; sash cramp; flue liner; purlin; water-table; wind turbine; low-e coating; vapour barrier.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Solar panel: collects solar radiation and converts it to heat; generally on a south-facing sloping roof, or on secure fixings at ground level; flat plate or evacuated tube; used with other heating; helps reduce CO₂. Dovetail halving joint: like a tee halving with a dovetail slope added, half the thickness taken from each piece; strong, resists pulling and has a large gluing area; slope 1:8 for hardwoods, 1:6 for softwoods. Sash cramp: a steel bar with a threaded mechanism at one end and a movable shoe, used to put pressure on wooden members while glue sets, as in furniture making; in various lengths. Flue liner: a conduit carrying smoke from the fire or stove, built in as the chimney is constructed or fitted to an existing chimney for a new stove; usually ceramic clay, or flexible stainless steel. Purlin: the member stretching under the rafters to support a traditional cut roof, typically 150 × 75 mm, carried on struts to an internal load-bearing wall or on an RSJ; it helps attic development. Water table: the natural level of underground water: rain percolates through the topsoil and subsoil; it rises and falls with rainfall, with springs appearing as it rises; below it water is held in aquifers reached by deep wells. Wind turbine: converts the energy of the wind into mechanical energy to generate electricity, small scale or commercial; a clean source of energy; blades, generator and support tower. Low-e coating: a very thin transparent metal or metal-oxide coating on the inner pane of double glazing that reflects heat back into the house while admitting solar gain; dearer, but reduces heat loss. Vapour barrier: a continuous membrane on the warm side of the insulation, slowing water vapour into it; used in timber frame walls, flat roofs and attic conversions; often part of insulated plasterboard.
